title: Debate & Discussion Skills

pts: Unstructured 'discuss this' tasks often let a few confident learners dominate while others stay silent.
Formal debate structures — assigned positions, timed turns, defined roles — distribute participation more evenly.
This connects to Unit 15's differentiation principles, applied to spoken-turn distribution specifically.

v: A class list; a tally sheet

items: Set a group of five learners an open discussion question for five minutes.
A colleague or learner observer tallies each turn on a sheet with the group’s names.
Repeat with a structured format: each learner has a numbered turn and one minute.
Compare the two tallies.
Discuss with colleagues: what did structure change?
Observers also note the kind of turn: new idea, agreement, disagreement, question.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Open discussion: Arjun 9, Meena 6, Farhan 2, Lakshmi 1, Sunil 0.
Structured round: Arjun 3, Meena 3, Farhan 3, Lakshmi 3, Sunil 2.

blocks.x: The structured round does not make Sunil fluent, but it gives him a guaranteed opening. The same principle of adapting task design to different learners appears in Unit 15.

body: Purpose: to show uneven and even participation. Content: two bar charts side by side with five names; the first has one tall bar and several short or empty ones, the second has bars of similar height. Style: clean, data-like. Board version: tally marks under five names.

items: Equity Maps (paid app for iPad) for tracking talk patterns [VERIFY current availability and pricing].

blocks.x: A paper tally sheet with names across the top.

points.sub: Arguing a side, not just stating one
pts: Assign learners a position to argue, sometimes deliberately against their own genuine opinion.
Arguing an assigned position builds strategic and discourse competence independent of personal conviction.
This also reduces the emotional stakes of genuine disagreement, supporting the safety principles of Unit 22.

items: Write a motion on the board (Mobile phones should be allowed in school).
Learners privately note their own opinion.
Give each learner a slip saying FOR or AGAINST, assigned randomly.
Learners with the same position prepare three reasons together.
Pairs of opposite positions present and respond to each other.
Finally, learners say whether hearing the other side changed their view.
Switch sides halfway: each learner must argue both positions.
Support: provide a list of possible reasons on each side.
Challenge: learners must anticipate and answer one counter-argument.

lines: T: You’re not telling me what you believe. You’re a lawyer for your side. Your job is to find the best reasons.
S1: But I’m against phones and I got FOR.
T: Good. That makes you a better lawyer: you already know the other side’s arguments.

blocks.x: Arguing an assigned position separates the argument from the arguer. A learner who is challenged is defending a position, not herself, which supports the classroom safety discussed in Unit 22.

body: Purpose: to show assigned positions. Content: a learner wearing a lawyer’s black coat over a school uniform, holding a card labelled ‘FOR’, while a small thought bubble shows her own view, ‘AGAINST’. Style: light, humorous. Board version: two hats labelled ‘FOR’ and ‘AGAINST’.

items: Wheel of Names (free) to assign positions randomly.

blocks.x: Folded FOR and AGAINST slips drawn from a box.

pts: Explicitly teach the structure of a spoken argument — claim, supporting reason, example or evidence.
This is Unit 33's genre awareness applied to the specific genre of argumentative discourse.
Model this structure with a short example before learners are expected to produce their own.

v: A three-part frame on the board

items: Model one argument aloud, pointing to the three parts on the board.
Learners identify the three parts in two more examples.
In pairs, learners build their own argument on a given topic, one part each, then combine them.
Pairs say their argument to another pair, who check that all three parts are present.
Collect good examples on the board for later use.
Add a fourth part, a response to an objection, at B2.
Support: sentence starters for each part.
Challenge: learners give two reasons, each with evidence.

blocks.x: A model argument (written for this book):

lines: Claim: Schools should have a daily reading period.
Reason: because reading regularly improves vocabulary and concentration.
Evidence: For example, in our school library club, members say they finish books much faster now.
I believe that… The main reason is… For example… This shows that…

blocks.x: This is genre awareness (Unit 33) applied to argument: a predictable structure that learners can learn, use and later vary.

body: Purpose: to show the parts of an argument. Content: a stool with a seat labelled ‘Claim’ and three legs, two labelled ‘Reason’ and ‘Evidence’, the third labelled ‘Response to objection’ drawn in a lighter colour as an optional extension. Style: simple, sturdy. Board version: a stool drawing.

items: Kialo Edu (free) for building visual argument maps with claims and reasons.

blocks.x: Three-colour argument strips on chart paper.

body: In the classical Indian tradition of vāda, structured debate was treated as a method of inquiry, with rules for stating a position, giving reasons and examples, and answering objections. Amartya Sen (2005) argues that this long habit of public reasoning is an important part of India’s intellectual heritage.

pts: Teach a functional toolkit of hedged disagreement, polite challenge, and concession language explicitly.
This connects to Unit 27's sociolinguistic competence — disagreement has cultural and register dimensions worth making explicit.
Without this toolkit, learners often either avoid disagreement entirely or express it too bluntly for the register.

items: Give groups phrase cards ranging from very direct to very softened disagreement.
Groups arrange them on a ladder from most polite to most direct.
Discuss which phrases suit which situations: a friend, a teacher, a formal debate.
Learners practise responding to provocative statements using a phrase from a given rung.
Add phrases for concession and agreement.
Compare how disagreement is softened in learners’ home languages; list equivalent phrases.
Support: fewer cards, with icons for polite and direct.
Challenge: add intonation practice; the same words can sound polite or rude.

lines: I see your point, but I’m not sure I agree.
That’s true to some extent, but…
I’m afraid I disagree.
I don’t think that’s right.
That’s wrong.
You’re right that… however…
Could you give an example of that?
I agree with Asha on one point, but…

blocks.x: Without this toolkit, learners tend to either avoid disagreeing or use the bluntest form they know. Many Indian languages soften disagreement with respect forms and indirect phrasing, and learners can transfer that awareness to English. Unit 53 returns to politeness theory in depth.

body: Purpose: to show a range of politeness. Content: a ladder with five rungs, each carrying a speech bubble phrase; the top rungs are shaded soft green, the bottom rung a strong red. A small figure is choosing a rung. Style: clear, colour-coded. Board version: a ladder with phrases.

items: Quizlet (free basic version) for phrase sets with example contexts.

blocks.x: Phrase cards on a string ladder on the classroom wall.

pts: A simple 'for and against' discussion in small groups works for lower levels and shorter class time.
A formal debate with timed speeches, rebuttal and a judged decision suits higher levels and more class time.
Match the format's complexity to the level, rather than defaulting to the most elaborate version for every class.

items: A2 option, four corners: learners move to corners labelled Strongly agree, Agree, Disagree, Strongly disagree, then give one reason each.
B1 option, for and against: small groups list reasons on each side, then decide as a group.
B2 option, a mini-debate: two teams of three, two-minute opening speeches, one-minute rebuttals, a class vote.
C1 option, formal debate: timed speeches, points of information, judges who give reasons for their decision.
Choose the simplest format that meets the lesson’s aim.
Fishbowl: an inner circle debates while an outer circle observes, then they swap.
Support: stay at the four-corners stage until learners can give reasons easily.
Challenge: add points of information, which require quick response.

lines: Team A opening (2 min) → Team B opening (2 min) → Preparation (2 min) → Team B rebuttal (1 min) → Team A rebuttal (1 min) → Class vote with one-sentence reasons.

blocks.x: With fifty learners and fixed benches, four corners can become ‘four rows’: learners stand in place and hold up a card showing their position.

body: Purpose: to show formats matched to level. Content: a staircase with four steps: four corners (A2), for and against (B1), mini-debate (B2), formal debate (C1). Each step has a small classroom icon. Style: clean, progressive. Board version: four steps.

items: Mentimeter (free plan) for quick opinion polls before and after a debate.
Classroomscreen (free basic version) for speech timers.

blocks.x: Position cards held up at benches; a teacher’s watch for timing.

pts: Assign explicit speaking roles or turn structures so quieter learners have a guaranteed opportunity to contribute.
A 'devil's advocate' or rotating chair role can be given specifically to learners who might otherwise stay silent.
This directly addresses the participation-imbalance problem unstructured discussion often produces.

v: Role cards: chair, devil’s advocate, summarizer, timekeeper

items: Form groups of five and give each learner a role card.
The chair invites each person to speak in turn and asks quieter members directly.
The devil’s advocate must challenge whatever the group seems to agree on.
The summarizer reports the group’s conclusion; the timekeeper keeps turns short.
Rotate roles every ten minutes or every lesson.
Give ‘talk tokens’: each learner has three tokens and places one on the bench each time they speak; no one can speak twice until everyone has used one.
Support: give quieter learners the chair or devil’s advocate role, which comes with a script of questions.
Challenge: the chair must also connect ideas (So Ravi and Nisha both think…).

lines: Let’s hear from everyone. Kavya, what do you think?
We haven’t heard from Imran yet.
Just to challenge that: what if…?
Someone could argue that…

blocks.x: The role gives a quiet learner permission to speak. The same learner who stays silent in open discussion may speak readily when it is her job to ask.

body: Purpose: to show structured roles. Content: five learners around a table, each with a small badge (‘Chair’, ‘Devil’s advocate’, ‘Summarizer’, ‘Timekeeper’, ‘Speaker’) and a circular arrow showing roles rotating. Style: warm, collaborative. Board version: a circle with five labels.

items: Canva for Education (free for teachers) for printable role badges.

blocks.x: Role badges made from card and safety pins; talk tokens from bottle caps.

pts: Note recurring language gaps — hedging, connectors, argument structure — during the debate for a post-task language-focus stage.
This mirrors Unit 28's task-cycle principle: language focus follows the communicative activity, informed by what it surfaced.
Avoid interrupting live debate for correction, protecting its communicative, fluency-building purpose.

items: During the debate, note recurring gaps: missing connectors, weak hedging, unclear structure.
Do not interrupt the debate for correction.
After the debate, write six sentences on the board: three good, three to improve.
Pairs improve the weaker sentences.
Teach one focused language point based on the most common gap, then give a short practice task.
Record the debate (with permission) and select examples from the recording.
Support: underline the problem in each sentence.
Challenge: learners find and improve the sentences themselves from a transcript extract.

lines: Phones are bad. Students are distracted. → Phones should be limited because students are easily distracted.
You are wrong. → I see your point, but I’m not sure that’s always true.
Good: ‘On the other hand, phones help with research.’

blocks.x: This follows the task cycle of Unit 28: communication first, then a language focus shaped by what the task revealed.

body: Purpose: to show language focus after a task. Content: a field of speech bubbles; a teacher with a basket picks some, which are then shown on a board, divided into ‘Keep’ and ‘Improve’. Style: gentle, agricultural metaphor. Board version: two columns headed ‘Keep’ and ‘Improve’.

items: A phone voice recorder app (free) to capture extracts for later analysis.

blocks.x: The teacher’s notebook, with a page divided into ‘Keep’ and ‘Improve’.

pts: Assess the quality of reasoning and turn-taking, not only fluency or grammatical accuracy.
This connects to Unit 27's discourse and strategic competence as explicit, assessable criteria.
Peer assessment of argument quality, structured with clear criteria, adds a valuable listening-with-purpose dimension too.

items: Share the criteria before the debate: reasoning, responding to others, turn-taking and language.
Assign some learners as judges for each round, rotating so everyone judges once.
Judges score each speaker and write one reason for each score.
Judges announce the result and explain it.
The teacher adds comments, focusing on reasoning and response.
Judges use a single criterion each and combine their scores.
Support: judges use a yes / partly / not yet scale.
Challenge: judges must quote one argument from each side.

blocks.x: A judge’s sheet (written for this book):

lines: Reasoning: Did the speaker give reasons and examples? 1 2 3
Response: Did the speaker answer the other side? 1 2 3
Turn-taking: Did the speaker let others speak and build on them? 1 2 3
Language: Was the speaker clear and polite? 1 2 3

blocks.x: These criteria draw on discourse and strategic competence (Unit 27). A fluent speaker who ignores opponents should not win automatically. Judging also gives listeners a purpose. Units 43 and 46 develop peer assessment and performance assessment further.

body: Purpose: to show peer assessment. Content: three learners at a judges’ table with score sheets, listening carefully; the speaker in front of them holds a card labelled ‘Claim, reason, evidence’. Style: respectful, clear. Board version: not applicable.

items: Google Forms (free) for judges’ score sheets that total automatically.

blocks.x: Paper judges’ sheets, collected and summarized by the teacher.

body: Next time you set an open discussion, add one structure only: a chair who must hear from every member before the group reaches a decision. Count how many learners speak, and compare with your last open discussion.

dek: Unit 39 of 100: structuring extended spoken interaction around genuine disagreement and reasoning — a distinct skill set from general conversation practice.

aims.x: This unit is about structured spoken argument: debate, discussion and the skills of disagreeing well in English. It treats these as a distinct skill set, different from general conversation, which needs explicit teaching of structure, functional language and turn-taking.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: explain why unstructured discussion often fails and how structure helps;
use assigned positions to lower the emotional stakes of disagreement;
teach the claim–reason–evidence structure of a spoken argument;
teach a functional toolkit for agreeing, disagreeing, challenging and conceding;
choose a debate or discussion format that suits the level and time available;
use roles and turn structures to balance participation;
plan a language-focus stage based on what a debate reveals;
assess reasoning and turn-taking as well as fluency and accuracy.

why: Why this matters. General 'discussion practice' often collapses into a few confident learners talking. Structured debate distributes participation and demands real reasoning in the target language.

background.x: Most teachers have tried the instruction ‘Discuss this in your groups’ and watched what happens: two or three confident learners talk, others nod, and some drift into another language or into silence. The problem is not that learners have nothing to say. It is that open discussion gives no structure for who speaks, when, and how to build on or oppose what others have said. Neil Mercer (1995, 2000) distinguished three kinds of group talk: disputational talk, in which speakers simply assert and reject; cumulative talk, in which they agree without examining ideas; and exploratory talk, in which they challenge each other’s ideas constructively, with reasons. Exploratory talk is the kind most linked to learning, and it rarely happens without teaching.

A spoken argument has a structure. Stephen Toulmin (1958) analysed arguments into a claim, the data that support it, and the warrant linking the two, with room for qualifiers and rebuttals. For language teaching, a simpler version works well: claim, reason, example or evidence. Disagreement also has a social shape. Conversation analysts have shown that in many contexts agreement is the ‘preferred’ response, while disagreement tends to be delayed, softened and accompanied by explanation (Pomerantz 1984). Brown and Levinson’s (1987) account of politeness explains why: disagreement threatens the other person’s face. Learners need language that lets them disagree clearly without sounding rude, which is a sociolinguistic skill (Unit 27) and a matter of culture (Unit 24).

India has a long tradition of public reasoning. Amartya Sen (2005) describes a heritage of argument and debate running through philosophical, religious and political life, from the dialogues of ancient texts to the councils called by Ashoka and Akbar. Many learners are also familiar with school elocution and debate competitions, though these often reward prepared speeches rather than listening and responding. The NEP 2020 emphasizes critical thinking and discussion-based learning (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020), and the NCF 2023 includes reasoning and respectful discussion among the capacities schooling should develop (NCERT 2023). Home languages help here: learners can build arguments in a stronger language first, and translate their best reasons into English. This unit shows how to turn debate from a performance for a few into structured practice for all.

items: Argument structure. Check whether learners’ spoken arguments include claim, reason and evidence.
Disagreement language. Listen for softened disagreement and concession phrases in use, not only in exercises.
Participation spread. Compare turn tallies across lessons to see whether structure is working.
Peer judgement. Review judges’ sheets for the quality of their reasons, which also shows listening comprehension.
What happens in your classes when you say ‘Discuss this’?
How do your learners disagree with each other, in English and in their home languages?
Have you ever asked learners to argue against their own opinion? How did they respond?
Which formats suit your class size and timetable?
Which learners never speak in discussion? What role could help them?
Do you assess reasoning, or only language?

terms.def: In a debate or discussion, a viewpoint that a learner is given to argue rather than one they personally hold; it separates the argument from the arguer and lowers the emotional stakes of disagreement.
The main position that a speaker or writer argues for; in the simplified claim–reason–evidence structure, it is supported by a reason and an example or evidence (Toulmin 1958).
A move in argument that accepts part of an opposing point before responding, such as ‘That is true, but…’; it makes a speaker sound reasonable and persuasive.
A person who argues against a position, not necessarily from belief, to test the strength of an argument and encourage deeper thinking; in class, the role can be assigned in discussions.
In a spoken or written argument, the facts, examples or data that support a reason and a claim. Learners practise the simple structure claim, reason, example or evidence.
Talk in which learners engage critically but constructively with each other’s ideas, giving reasons, asking questions and thinking aloud together (Barnes 1976; Mercer 2000).

A person’s public self-image. Positive face is the wish to be liked and approved of; negative face is the wish not to be imposed upon. Requests, criticisms and disagreement threaten face (Brown and Levinson 1987).
Using language to soften a claim or show caution, such as may, seems, perhaps or it could be argued. It is important in academic writing and in polite disagreement.

In a spoken or written argument, the statement that explains why a claim should be accepted. Learners are taught the simple structure claim–reason–evidence, for example ‘Schools should have libraries because…’, followed by an example.

In argument and debate, a response that challenges or answers the opposing side’s claims. Toulmin (1958) included rebuttals in his model of argument; in class, a mini-debate can give each team a short, timed rebuttal turn.
